lesson.title: Future Gym
lesson.subtitle: Near-future sentences chaining je vais / tu vas / on va with converted verbs.

hook.title: Chaining Near-Future Plans With Your -ation Verbs
hook.content: Combine Topic 12's near future (aller) with Topic 3's -ation verb engine (confirmer, organiser, visiter, préparer, réserver, célébrer): only aller conjugates; the second verb stays parked in its bare -er infinitive form!

footnotes.title: Negating the near future: wrap aller, leave the infinitive outside
footnotes.content: In On ne va pas attendre ('We are not going to wait'), ne...pas wraps only the conjugated auxiliary va!

pattern.title: aller (Conjugated) + Infinitive (Parked)
pattern.content: Run the near-future formula across positive, negative, and question sentences.
pattern.linguist_note: Periphrastic future with aller + infinitive is the default spoken future for planned events.
pattern.trap_note: Never put pas after the infinitive (*Je ne vais partir pas) — pas hugs the form of aller (Je ne vais pas partir)!

exercises.prompt: Match each near-future plan with its French sentence:

matching_pairs.english: I am going to prepare the coffee
We (on) are going to organize the dinner
We (nous) are going to visit the city

exercises.target_answer: Je vais préparer le café, Tu vas confirmer ?, On va organiser le dîner, Nous allons visiter la ville, Vous allez réserver ?
exercises.meaning: I am going to prepare the coffee, Are you going to confirm?, We (on) are going to organize the dinner, We (nous) are going to visit the city, Are you (polite) going to reserve?
exercises.explanation: Every person of aller chains directly to the bare infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Negate 'On va attendre' ('We are going to wait'):
exercises.meaning: We are not going to wait
exercises.explanation: ne...pas wraps the conjugated auxiliary va; attendre waits outside.

exercises.prompt: Build the near future: 'She is going to celebrate' (Elle + va + celebrate):

exercises.idea: I am going to prepare the reservation tomorrow
cues: I am going to prepare → Je vais préparer
the reservation tomorrow → la réservation demain
exercises.target_answer: Je vais préparer la réservation demain
exercises.meaning: I am going to prepare the reservation tomorrow
exercises.explanation: préparer stays in its infinitive form after Je vais.

diagnosis.cue: Keep préparer in the infinitive after Je vais.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: You are going to visit the university tomorrow
exercises.explanation: allez (/ale/) and visiter (/vizite/) both end in /e/.
exercises.affirmation: You distinguished conjugated allez (-ez) from infinitive visiter (-er)!

summary.outcome: Chain aller across all persons with converted -er/-ir/-re infinitives in positive, negative, and question sentences.

use_example.german: Ce soir, on va préparer un bon dîner et célébrer.
use_example.english: Tonight, we're going to prepare a good dinner and celebrate.

summary.takeaway: Conjugate aller, park the infinitive, and hug aller with ne...pas when negating.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([13] à, de, chez): see how Future Gym leads directly into à, de, chez.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I am going to prepare the reservation tomorrow" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je vais préparer la réservation demain
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je vais préparer la réservation demain" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Future Gym.

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

je_vais.etymology_derivation: vais is aller's only irregular card in je; with an infinitive after it, it makes the future.

allons.etymology_derivation: Regular stem all- returns in nous allons and vous allez.

allez.etymology_derivation: Also shouted at sports matches: 'Allez !' ('Come on!').

confirmer.etymology_derivation: confirmation → confirmer. Strip -ation, bolt on -er (pronounced /e/), and the noun becomes the verb.

organiser.etymology_derivation: organisation → organiser. One S in French, even where English writes Z.

visiter.etymology_derivation: visitation → visiter. The rare English noun unlocks the everyday verb: don't decide too quickly that you can't say it.

demain.context_translation: Tomorrow, I'm going to visit Lyon.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
